title: Fiber Cement Board vs Plywood: Exterior and Facade Applications Compared
description: Technical comparison of fiber cement board and plywood for exterior walls, ventilated facades, and wet rooms. Fire class, moisture resistance, weight, and CE certification compared.
author: Terasun Europe Technical Team
body:
## Fiber Cement Board vs Plywood: Exterior and Facade Applications Compared

Plywood and fiber cement board both appear in architects' specifications for exterior wall sheathing, facade systems, and wet rooms. They differ fundamentally in material composition, fire behaviour, moisture performance, and regulatory compliance. This guide compares them for common European construction applications.

---

### Material Composition

**Plywood** is a wood-based panel product manufactured by bonding thin veneers of wood with resin under heat and pressure. Exterior-grade plywood uses phenol-formaldehyde or melamine-urea resin for improved moisture resistance. It is an organic, combustible material.

**Fiber cement board** (FCB) is an inorganic product manufactured from Portland cement, inorganic fillers, and reinforcing fibres. It contains no wood, no organic binders, and no asbestos. It is non-combustible.

---

### Fire Performance

This is the most critical difference for building regulations compliance:

| Product | Reaction to Fire | Euroclass |
|---|---|---|
| Plywood (standard) | Combustible | Class D or E |
| Plywood (fire-retardant treated) | Improved, still combustible | Class C–D |
| Terasun TSM Fiber Cement | Non-combustible | **Class A1** |

In Europe, facade materials for buildings above 18 m height are typically required to be **Class A1 or A2** under the Construction Products Regulation and national transpositions. Standard and even fire-retardant-treated plywood does not meet this requirement.

Terasun TSM fiber cement board achieves **A1** — non-combustible with very limited smoke production and no flaming droplets or particles — and the tested wall assembly reaches **E 120 / EI 90 / EW 120** for fire compartmentalisation.

---

### Moisture Performance

Exterior-grade plywood (EN 636 Class 3) has improved moisture resistance but is still susceptible to:
- **Delamination** at cut edges when repeatedly wetted
- **Biological attack** — mould, fungi, and blue stain if moisture content stays above 18–20%
- **Dimensional movement** — swelling and shrinkage with moisture cycling

Fiber cement board under **EN 12467 Category A** is:
- Dimensionally stable when fully saturated
- Immune to mould and biological attack (no organic content)
- Suitable for continuous exterior exposure and direct tile adhesive application in wet rooms

---

### Weight Comparison

| Product | Thickness | Weight (kg/m²) |
|---|---|---|
| Structural plywood (EN 636-3) | 18 mm | 10–12 |
| Structural plywood (EN 636-3) | 12 mm | 7–8 |
| Terasun TSM Fiber Cement | 12 mm | **9.96** |
| Terasun TSM Fiber Cement | 8 mm | approx. 6.6 |

At 12 mm, the two products are comparable in weight. For facade applications where 8–10 mm fiber cement board is typically used, the weight advantage over structural plywood becomes more pronounced.

---

### Regulatory and Certification Comparison

| Property | Plywood (EN 636) | Fiber Cement Board (EN 12467) |
|---|---|---|
| CE standard | EN 636 | **EN 12467** |
| European Technical Assessment | Not applicable | **ETA 24/0895** |
| Declaration of Performance | EN 636 DoP | **DoP TRS-20250610F** |
| EPD (environmental) | Varies | **EPD-IES-0018268** |
| LEED/BREEAM suitability | Wood credits | **EPD credits + fire class** |

---

### Application Guide: Which to Choose?

**Use plywood when:**
- Structural sheathing in protected timber frame construction (dry, internal)
- Roof decking under membranes where fire class D is acceptable
- Cost is the primary driver and fire/moisture performance requirements are low
- Curved surfaces requiring flexibility

**Use fiber cement board when:**
- **Ventilated facade cladding** — all climates, all building heights
- **High-rise or public buildings** — where A1/A2 facade materials are required
- **Fire-rated wall assemblies** — E120/EI90/EW120
- **Wet rooms and bathrooms** — tile backing and sheathing
- **Steel frame and modular buildings** — non-combustible structural sheathing
- **Render carrier boards** — substrate for exterior mineral render
- **LEED, BREEAM, DGNB projects** — EPD documentation available

---

### Cost Considerations

Plywood is generally lower in material cost. However, the total installed cost comparison must account for:
- **Fire treatment costs**: fire-retardant-treated plywood significantly increases cost and may still not achieve A2
- **Maintenance**: plywood facades require more frequent maintenance and re-painting due to moisture movement
- **Compliance costs**: using non-compliant materials in fire-regulated zones creates legal and insurance liability
- **System longevity**: fiber cement board systems last 30–50 years without biological degradation

---

*Terasun TSM fiber cement board is CE-certified under EN 12467 (CE 1023-CPR-1565 P), with ETA 24/0895 and EPD-IES-0018268. Contact Terasun Europe for technical data sheets, samples, and pricing.*

faq.q: Can plywood be used on ventilated facades?
faq.a: Exterior-grade plywood can be used on low-rise ventilated facades where fire class D is acceptable. For buildings over 18 m or where A2 materials are required, plywood does not meet European fire regulations for facades.

faq.q: Is fiber cement board heavier than plywood?
faq.a: At 12 mm, Terasun TSM fiber cement board weighs 9.96 kg/m², which is comparable to 12 mm structural plywood at 7–8 kg/m². However, facade applications typically use 8–10 mm fiber cement board, which is lighter than structural plywood at equivalent spans.

faq.q: Does fiber cement board need surface treatment for exterior use?
faq.a: Terasun TSM fiber cement board is suitable for exterior use without additional sealing. For aesthetic finishing, it can be painted with standard exterior mineral or silicone paints. Cut edges should be sealed with an appropriate primer or edge sealant.
